summary: Defines the IPsec Domain of Interpretation, which tells ISAKMP how to negotiate security associations for IP security. It assigns the identifiers and formats that ISAKMP needs for IPsec. It is now historic, replaced by RFC 4306.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people need to agree what words mean before they can make a deal. This document is the dictionary that lets computers agree on the meaning of security terms for IPsec.

questions: what is the ipsec domain of interpretation
what encryption algorithms does ipsec support
subtitle: Defines how ISAKMP negotiates IP security parameters and encryption algorithms.

tldr.problem: ISAKMP is a framework for negotiating security associations, but it needs a domain-specific interpretation to be used with IP security. Without one, there is no standard way for IPsec implementations to agree on which algorithms to use.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the IPsec Domain of Interpretation (DOI), which specifies the naming scheme for IPsec protocols (AH, ESP, IPCOMP), lists the approved encryption and authentication transforms with their identifiers, and defines how ISAKMP payloads encode IPsec-specific information.
tldr.outcome: The IPsec DOI became the standard way for systems to negotiate IP security associations, but this RFC is now Historic and replaced by RFC 4306, which reflects updates to IPsec standards and key exchange methods.

today: RFC 2407 is Historic and has been replaced by RFC 4306, which updates the IPsec DOI with stronger algorithms and alignment to modern IPsec and IKE standards.

sections.title: Domain of Interpretation for ISAKMP
sections.content:
The Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol (ISAKMP) defines a framework for negotiating security associations and establishing cryptographic keys. However, ISAKMP itself is generic and does not define which protocols, algorithms, and cryptographic transforms to use.

A Domain of Interpretation (DOI) adds the specific rules and definitions for one application area. This RFC defines the IPsec DOI, which tells ISAKMP how to negotiate security for IP packets sent between hosts and firewalls. The DOI specifies the protocol identifiers (names and numbers), the encryption and authentication transforms, the format of security association payloads, and the policy requirements that IPsec implementations must support.
sections.plainLanguage: ISAKMP is a tool for making agreements. The IPsec DOI tells the tool how to make the right kind of agreement for protecting IP traffic.

sections.title: IPsec Protocols and Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC assigns identifier numbers to the IPsec security protocols that ISAKMP negotiates:

PROTO_ISAKMP (1) is used for Phase I negotiation of the IKE (Oakley) key exchange protocol itself. PROTO_IPSEC_AH (2) specifies the Authentication Header protocol, which provides origin authentication, integrity protection, and replay detection for IP packets. PROTO_IPSEC_ESP (3) specifies the Encapsulating Security Payload protocol, which provides confidentiality (encryption) for IP packets. PROTO_IPCOMP (4) specifies IP payload compression.

For confidentiality, implementations must support ESP. For authentication, they must support AH with HMAC-MD5 or HMAC-SHA-1. The Situation field (a 4-octet bitmask) allows implementations to negotiate support for labeled secrecy and labeled integrity in high-security environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Each type of protection gets a number: AH for signatures, ESP for encryption, IPCOMP for compression. Systems negotiate which ones they will use.

sections.title: Encryption and Authentication Transforms
sections.content:
For AH (authentication), the RFC defines AH_MD5, AH_SHA, and AH_DES transforms. All implementations must support AH_MD5 with HMAC-MD5-96 and AH_SHA with HMAC-SHA-1-96 for integrity protection.

For ESP (encryption), the RFC lists many transforms: ESP_DES, ESP_3DES, ESP_RC5, ESP_IDEA, ESP_CAST, ESP_BLOWFISH, and others. All implementations must support ESP_DES with HMAC-MD5 for confidentiality and authentication combined. The RFC notes that DES is the minimum, but implementations are encouraged to support 3DES (triple-DES) for stronger encryption.

For IPCOMP, the transforms are IPCOMP_DEFLATE (zlib deflate compression) and IPCOMP_LZS (Stac LZS compression).
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists which codes (encryption algorithms) are allowed and which must be supported. DES is minimum, but stronger codes like 3DES are recommended.

sections.title: SA Negotiation and Key Management
sections.content:
The RFC defines Security Association (SA) attributes that ISAKMP uses during Phase II negotiation to agree on the parameters of an IPsec connection. These include SA Life Type (time-based or byte-count-based), SA Life Duration (how long the keys remain valid), Encapsulation Mode (tunnel or transport mode), Authentication Algorithm (which signature algorithm to use), Key Length (size of the encryption key), and others.

Systems must implement key management policies including certificate management for authentication, static keying for pre-shared secrets, and policies for which peers are trusted. The RFC notes considerations for protecting static keys and managing certificates, though these are implementation choices not mandated by the protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Before encrypting, systems negotiate the lifetime of the keys, which algorithms to use, and how long before new keys are needed.

sections.title: Status and Obsolescence
sections.content:
RFC 2407 is now Historic, having been replaced by RFC 4306. The replacement reflects updates to the IPsec architecture, including changes to the mandatory algorithms, the deprecation of DES due to cryptanalysis, and alignment with changes to the IKE protocol itself.

This RFC made important early definitions of IPsec negotiation that saw wide deployment, but as IPsec standards evolved, a new DOI document was needed to keep pace with cryptographic best practices and protocol improvements.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defined how IPsec systems negotiate encryption with each other, but better methods came along and it was replaced.
